title: Figma Shares Drop Despite Earnings Beat as AI‑Driven Long‑Term Growth Strategy Takes Center Stage
body:
Figma’s shares slid 7% in after‑hours trading on Thursday, even as the design‑software firm posted third‑quarter results that beat analysts’ expectations. The dip came after the company announced a strategic shift: it will expand access to its suite of artificial‑intelligence tools without raising prices, a move aimed at driving longer‑term growth rather than delivering an immediate earnings pop. Investors, however, appear skeptical that the AI‑centric strategy will translate into faster top‑line expansion, prompting the stock’s modest retreat.

The earnings release showed revenue of $375 million for the quarter, up 31% year‑over‑year and comfortably ahead of the consensus forecast of $360 million compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.31, surpassing the $0.27 estimate. Despite the beat, the company’s guidance for the upcoming fiscal year—projecting revenue of $1.6 billion, a 28% increase—was viewed as modest relative to the lofty growth rates the market had been pricing in for a design‑platform that has become a staple for tech and creative teams worldwide.

Figma’s decision to open its AI features to all paying customers at no extra cost marks a departure from the typical “premium‑add‑on” model used by many SaaS firms. The firm’s AI capabilities, which include generative design suggestions, automatic layout adjustments, and smart content creation, have been in beta for the past six months. By removing a price barrier, Figma hopes to accelerate adoption across its expanding enterprise base and embed AI deeper into everyday design workflows. “We want AI to be a productivity multiplier for every designer, not a gated feature for a few,” said CEO Dylan Field in the earnings call.

Analysts are divided on whether the strategy will boost the company’s revenue trajectory. Some argue that broader AI usage could increase user stickiness, reduce churn, and open cross‑selling opportunities for Figma’s collaboration and prototyping tools. Others caution that the move could compress margins, especially if the AI infrastructure costs rise faster than anticipated. “The upside is clear—more AI engagement can drive higher license renewals—but the downside is that we’re essentially giving away a high‑margin capability for free,” noted a senior equity analyst at a West Coast boutique firm.

The market’s reaction also reflects lingering concerns about competition. Adobe, the industry behemoth, has been integrating generative AI across its Creative Cloud suite, while newer entrants such as Canva and Sketch are rolling out their own AI‑enhanced features. Figma’s pricing model, which charges per seat rather than per feature, has traditionally been a differentiator, but the AI arms race could erode that advantage if rivals can match functionality without sacrificing profitability.

Looking ahead, Figma’s roadmap includes a deeper integration of AI into its collaborative environment, enabling real‑time design suggestions during live editing sessions. The company also plans to expand its marketplace for third‑party plugins, many of which will leverage its AI engine. If these initiatives succeed, they could unlock new revenue streams and cement Figma’s position as the go‑to platform for modern, AI‑augmented design work. For now, investors will be watching the next quarter closely to see whether the AI rollout translates into higher usage metrics and, ultimately, stronger financial performance. The next earnings report will likely determine whether the market’s cautious stance is justified or if Figma’s long‑term vision begins to bear fruit.
